Yates, with a 35-year career spanning various industries, champions the transformative power of technology to drive societal and economic progress. His current focus aligns with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology's recent advisory on GenAI deployment, emphasizing the need for explicit government approval, transparency, and bias prevention. Yates' initiative at Presight is pivotal at a time when the Indian government mandates strict guidelines for the deployment of AI technologies. According to recent regulations, platforms using AI models under testing, such as large language models or GenAI software, must secure government consent before public release. Yates believes that these measures will foster responsible AI use, ensuring that digital innovations serve the public interest without compromising ethical standards. The advisory from the Ministry outlines a clear path for AI development and deployment but also presents challenges for technology leaders like Yates. Ensuring AI technologies are devoid of bias, fully transparent, and compliant with regulatory demands requires diligent oversight. Yet, Yates views these hurdles as opportunities to demonstrate how responsible AI can enhance government services, improve decision-making, and contribute to a smarter, safer society. Yates emphasizes the importance of generative AI in revolutionizing public sector operations. His commitment to leveraging technology for positive social impact is evident in his work at Presight, where the focus is on utilizing GenAI to solve complex challenges in public safety, smart cities, and beyond. As the government tightens its grip on AI deployment, Yates’ role becomes increasingly crucial in navigating the evolving landscape, ensuring technology's potential is harnessed for the greater good. At the heart of Yates' mission is a conviction that technology, when guided by clear ethical standards and regulatory compliance, can be a force for good. With the Indian government setting a precedent for AI oversight, Yates' leadership at Presight positions him as a key player in shaping the future of government service delivery through technological innovation. title: GenAI startups don’t need to seek govt nod before launch, advisory only for Big Tech: Rajeev Chandrasekhar | Business News - The Indian Express
text:
The IT Ministry’s recent advisory to generative artificial intelligence (AI) companies which needed them to seek permission from the government before deploying “untested” AI systems only applies to big technology companies and not to start-ups, Minister of State (MoS) for Electronics and IT Rajeev Chandrasekhar has clarified. “Advisory is aimed at the significant platforms and permission seeking from MeitY is only for large platforms and will not apply to startups… is aimed at untested AI platforms from deploying on Indian Internet,” Chandrasekhar said in a post on social media platform X. At the time of issuing the advisory, the government had not explicitly mentioned that the conditions will only apply to bigger companies and not smaller businesses. However, since the government’s advisory was in many ways to limit the impact content from such platforms could have on the upcoming Lok Sabha elections, it is unclear why an exemption to start-ups has been offered, given that their systems are also prone to generating inaccurate information. The Indian Express had recently reported about Ola’s beta generative AI offering Krutrim’s hallucinations. Chandrasekhar added that the process of seeking permission, labelling of platforms that are under testing and consent-based disclosure to users is an “insurance policy to platforms who can otherwise be sued by consumers”. With Lok Sabha elections set to be announced soon, the IT Ministry on Friday had sent an advisory to generative AI companies like Google and OpenAI and to those running such platforms — including foundational models and wrappers — that that their services should not generate responses that are illegal under Indian laws or “threaten the integrity of the electoral process”. Platforms that currently offer “under-testing/unreliable” AI systems or large language models to Indian users must explicitly seek permission from the Centre before doing so and appropriately label the possible and inherent “fallibility or unreliability of the output generated”. As per the advisory, the government also wants these platforms to add in a traceability requirement by adding an identifiable marker to content they generate in a way that can be traced back to the person who has instructed the service to create pieces of misinformation or deepfakes. Google’s AI platform Gemini had recently come under fire from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) for answers generated by the platform on a question about Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Outputs generated by such platforms depend on a number of factors including the underlying training data that has been scraped from the vast swathes of the Internet and algorithmic filters that are added on top of that: a number of instances of errors — called hallucinations — generated by these platforms have been reported across the world can typically be attributed to shortcomings in these factors. “Where any intermediary through its software or any other computer resource permits or facilitates synthetic creation, generation or modification of a text, audio, visual or audio-visual information, in such a manner that such information may be used potentially as misinformation or deepfake… is labelled or embedded with a permanent unique metadata or identifier… (to) identify the user of the software,” the advisory had said. Signup    Follow Us India Introduces Mandatory MeitY Approval for AI, GenAI Model Deployment to Ensure Ethical Use In a groundbreaking move on March 3, 2024, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) announced that prior approval is now required for companies deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) models. This regulation aims to foster responsible and ethical utilization of AI technologies amidst growing concerns over data privacy, security, and AI's societal impacts. The decision underscores the government's dedication to balancing technological progress with public interest protection. Under the new mandate, all companies operating in India that wish to integrate AI and GenAI models into their operations must undergo a comprehensive evaluation by MeitY. This process will assess the technology's societal impact, ethical standards adherence, and compliance with existing laws. This move is part of a broader global trend towards establishing clear guidelines for AI development and deployment, addressing challenges like algorithmic bias and ethical concerns about autonomous systems. The Economic Times highlights that the MeitY approval requirement applies to both large corporations and startups, ensuring fair competition and adherence to the same standards across the board. This proactive approach by the government has been welcomed by experts, who emphasize the importance of transparency, accountability, and trust in AI technology deployment across various sectors, including healthcare, finance, and education. While the immediate effects of this regulatory landscape on AI development and deployment in India are yet to be fully realized, the MeitY approval process initiates industry-wide discussions on ethical considerations, responsible AI practices, and the necessity for collaborative efforts between the government, industry, and academia. This regulation marks a significant step towards shaping a comprehensive ethical and legal framework for AI technologies, aiming to maximize AI's potential benefits while minimizing its risks and negative societal impacts.
